sections.heading: Every step, including the awkward ones
sections.intro: Most systems are designed around the order that goes right. Here is what happens at each stage, and what the platform does when something changes, arrives short or gets disputed.

items.title: The order comes in
items.module: Web store · Dealer portal · Club stores
items.text: Every channel writes to the same orders, stock and customer records.
steps: Shoppers buy on your web store or their club's store, with sizes filled in from their Locker Room
Dealers order at their contract prices by size matrix, quick order or CSV upload
Club members join their club with a club code and order their team's kit
exceptions: A trade order goes over the account's credit limit → it waits for approval instead of going through
A dealer isn't ready to submit → the order is saved as a draft or template and finished later
A promo code or voucher doesn't apply to the product → it's declined, and the failed attempt is recorded
A voucher covers part of the order → the rest is paid by card or PayPal on the same order
The item is made to order → the order is taken now and made once the pre-order window closes

items.title: Sales order and ERP
items.text: The order is confirmed, the customer is told, and the sales order goes to your ERP.
steps: Order confirmation sent to the customer
Sales order sent to your ERP
The request and the ERP's response are both kept against the order
exceptions: Your ERP rejects the order or doesn't answer → the error is logged against the order and visible in the admin, so nothing fails silently
You don't run an ERP yet → the platform works without one, and an ERP can be connected later

items.title: Purchase orders from sales
items.text: Sales that need buying in roll up by product, size, club and team, ready to become purchase orders.
steps: POs are created back to back from sales orders, or pooled across many orders
Grouped the way you buy: by supplier and product type, or one PO per B2B sales order
Freight mode set per PO
Each PO is approved before it's sent
exceptions: The item is already in stock → no PO is needed; it's picked from stock
The pre-order window is still open → the sales wait and are pooled when it closes
The same sale must not be ordered twice → each sales line is linked to the PO line that covers it
The PO needs editing → change it while it's a draft; it locks once the supplier acknowledges it

items.title: The supplier acknowledges
items.text: Suppliers work in their own portal, not your inbox.
steps: The supplier is notified by email and in their portal
They acknowledge POs one at a time or in bulk
Your team is notified when a PO is acknowledged
exceptions: The supplier can't meet the date or quantity → they request a change, you accept or reject it, and they're told either way
The PO is cancelled → its lines are closed in your ERP as well

items.title: Production and artwork
items.text: Progress is recorded size by size, so you can see what's ready before it ships.
steps: The production workbench shows ordered and prepared quantities per size
Suppliers can update it in the portal or by exporting and importing Excel
Artwork and design proofs are approved in the platform
exceptions: The artwork needs changes → you request changes and the supplier uploads a revision; production goes ahead on the approved version
Only part of the order is ready → the rest stays open on the PO

items.title: Shipping
items.text: Suppliers create shipments with cartons, tracking and documents.
steps: One shipment can cover several POs
Cartons, tracking numbers and documents are attached to the shipment
With drop shipping switched on, suppliers can ship straight to your customer
exceptions: Only part of a PO ships → the PO shows as partially shipped and the rest ships later
The wrong document was uploaded → it's removed and replaced
A shipment has to be redone → a replacement shipment is created

items.title: Supplier invoices
items.text: Invoices are built from what actually shipped, so checking them is quick.
steps: A draft invoice is created when a shipment is dispatched, from the quantities shipped at the PO's prices
One invoice per shipment, with the supplier's own number or one generated for them
Your team is emailed when a shipment is dispatched
You approve the invoice for payment
exceptions: The invoice doesn't match → you dispute it with a reason, and the supplier revises and resubmits
The same invoice number is used twice → it's rejected
The supplier submitted too early → they withdraw the submission and fix it
A supplier changes their bank details → the change waits for your approval before it reaches your ERP

items.title: Receive, dispatch and returns
items.text: Goods are received against the PO, then picked and sent to the customer.
steps: Your warehouse or 3PL receives against the PO, in full or in part
Customer orders are picked, packed and dispatched with tracking
Customers see every order in their order history
exceptions: A delivery arrives short → what arrived is recorded, and the balance stays open
A customer wants to return something → the return is reviewed in the admin, then refunded or given back as a gift voucher

sections.heading: Seasons, squads and sizes don't fit a standard online store
sections.body:
Sport runs on seasons, not the calendar year. Cricket clubs need their kit before the first ball of summer, while hockey peaks in winter. Miss the window and the stock sits in the warehouse until next year.

Every buyer also needs something different. Fans want the official look and stock that's ready to ship. Clubs want their own range, personalised with each player's name and number. Dealers want trade prices, credit terms and a fast way to reorder.

A standard online store handles one of these well. StacCraft was built for all three, alongside a national sporting brand that sells to all three every week.

article.author: StacCraft team
article.excerpt: Club stores are where teamwear brands win or lose a season. Here's how to set them up so clubs, players and your team all do less admin.

sections.standfirst: Most teamwear suppliers don't lose money on the kit. They lose it on the admin around the kit: chasing sizes, re-keying orders and fixing mistakes after the season has started.
takeaways: Give every club its own store, range and season window, not a shared order form
Capture sizes and jersey details once, and reuse them every season
Close each order window on a date, then turn the orders into purchase orders in one step
Measure the hours your team spends per club, and aim to halve them
sections.body:
## Why spreadsheets break at club scale
A spreadsheet works for one club. At twenty clubs it becomes a part-time job, and at a hundred it becomes the reason your best people leave. Every club sends its order in a slightly different format, sizes arrive as free text, and somebody has to type the lot into your ordering system before a single garment is made.

The cost isn't only time. Each re-key is a chance to get a size, a name or a number wrong, and a misprinted playing shirt is expensive to fix in the middle of a season.

## Give every club its own store
The single biggest improvement is to stop collecting orders and start letting players buy. A club store gives each club its own branded page, its own range and its own prices, while your team manages everything from one admin.

- Each club sees only its own kit, in its own colours
- Teams within a club (for example U14 Girls) get the right items and sizes
- Players pay for their own kit, so the club treasurer isn't chasing money
- Club codes let new players join the right club without your team creating accounts

## Capture size data once
Size and personalisation data is the most valuable thing a teamwear supplier holds, and the most often lost. Ask for it once, store it against the player, and fill it in for them next season.

> Players who find their sizes and jersey number already filled in finish their order in a fraction of the time, and they come back.

In StacCraft, this is what the [Locker Room](#locker-room) does: it keeps each member's sizes, jersey name and number, and shows which pieces of the required kit they already own.

## Run the season on a timetable
Clubs buy in seasons, so your store should too. Set an opening and closing date for each club's order window and tell the clubs early. When the window closes:

1. The orders are locked, so nothing changes under you
2. Sales are rolled up by product, colour and size
3. Purchase orders go to suppliers in the same size breakdown your customers chose

That last step is where most of the hours disappear. If your team is still building purchase orders from an export, read [Pre-orders to purchase orders](#insights-preorders-to-pos).

## What to measure
Pick three numbers and track them each season:

- **Hours of admin per club**, from range set-up to delivery
- **Order errors** found after production starts
- **Days from window close to purchase order sent**

If any of these is going up as you add clubs, your process won't scale. That's the point to change it, not after the next season goes wrong.

article.author: StacCraft team
article.excerpt: Made-to-order kit is profitable when buying follows selling. How to turn a closed pre-order window into accurate purchase orders in minutes.

sections.standfirst: Pre-orders let you sell before you buy. The catch is the step in the middle, where somebody turns hundreds of orders into purchase orders by hand.
takeaways: Treat the pre-order close date as the start of buying, not the end of selling
Group purchase orders by supplier and product type, and keep sizes intact
Send POs through a supplier portal so acknowledgements and changes are tracked
Check invoices against what was shipped, not what was ordered
sections.body:
## The hidden cost of pre-orders
Pre-orders are the safest way to sell made-to-order apparel: the customer has paid before you commit to stock. But many businesses lose that advantage in the hand-off between sales and buying. Orders are exported, pivoted in a spreadsheet, split by supplier and typed into purchase orders, often days after the window closed.

Every day lost there is a day added to the customer's wait, and every manual step is a chance to order the wrong size run.

## Build purchase orders from sales, not exports
The better pattern is to generate purchase orders directly from the sales they fulfil:

1. Close the pre-order window on a fixed date
2. Roll up the sold lines by product, colour and size
3. Group them into purchase orders by supplier, and by product type if your suppliers make different things in different places
4. Review, approve and send

Because each purchase order line points back to the sales lines it covers, you can always answer the question every customer eventually asks: where is my order?

## Keep the supplier in the loop
A purchase order sent by email is a purchase order you'll chase by email. A supplier portal changes that. Suppliers acknowledge orders, request changes such as a new delivery date, record what they've produced by size, and mark shipments as dispatched, all against the original PO.

- You see what's acknowledged, what's late and what's shipped in one place
- Change requests are approved or declined, with a record of who decided
- Part shipments are normal, not an exception you track on paper

## Match the invoice to the shipment
The last step is the one accounts teams dread: checking the supplier's invoice. Compare it with what was actually shipped and the unit costs on the purchase order, not with the original order quantity. Differences become a dispute the supplier can see and fix, instead of an email thread.

> If your team can't tell you within a minute which pre-orders are still waiting on a supplier, the process needs fixing before the next window opens.

See how this works end to end on our [supply chain page](#procurement).

article.author: StacCraft team
article.excerpt: Connecting a web store to Sage X3 goes wrong when everything syncs both ways. A simple rule for deciding which system owns which data.

sections.standfirst: Most ERP integration problems aren't technical. They come from never deciding which system is in charge of each piece of data.
takeaways: Give every type of data exactly one owner
Post orders and purchase orders to the ERP, don't edit them there
Log every exchange, and retry failures automatically
Plan for the ERP being unavailable, because it sometimes will be
sections.body:
## One owner for every piece of data
Before connecting anything, write down every type of data that moves between your store and Sage X3, and name the system that owns it. The owner is where the data is created and changed. The other system receives a copy.

A typical split for apparel and sporting brands looks like this:

- **Sage X3 owns** customers' credit terms, cost prices, the chart of accounts and financial postings
- **The commerce platform owns** the online catalogue, product content, images, promotions and the shopping experience
- **Shared, one way at a time:** stock levels flow from the warehouse system, sales orders and purchase orders flow into Sage X3

If both systems can change the same field, they will eventually disagree, and nobody will know which is right.

## Orders go in, they don't come back out
Sales orders and purchase orders should be created in the commerce platform and posted to Sage X3, where finance works with them. Avoid editing a posted order in both places. If something has to change, change it at the source and post the update.

## Expect failures and log everything
Integrations fail: a customer record is missing, a product code doesn't exist yet, or the ERP is down for maintenance. A good integration:

1. Logs every exchange with the reference, time and result
2. Retries temporary failures on its own
3. Shows the failures that need a person in a list your team actually checks
4. Never creates the same order twice when a retry succeeds

> The question to ask any integration partner: "show me the log of the last 100 orders, including the ones that failed."

## Approvals for sensitive changes
Some changes are too risky to sync automatically. Supplier bank details are the classic example: a fraudulent change request is one of the most common payment scams. Changes like this should wait for approval before they reach the ERP.

Read more on our [integrations page](#integrations).

article.author: StacCraft team
article.excerpt: Search still drives more ready-to-buy shoppers than any other channel. A practical checklist for product pages, collections, technical SEO and AI search.

sections.standfirst: Shoppers who search for a product by name are ready to buy. This checklist covers what a sporting goods or teamwear store needs to rank for those searches, and to be described accurately by AI assistants.
takeaways: Write unique titles and descriptions for every product and collection
Add structured data for products, prices, stock and reviews
Keep filtered and sorted pages out of search results with canonical URLs
Make sure AI assistants can understand what you sell
sections.body:
## Product pages
Product pages are where most sales start, and most stores neglect them. For every product:

- A unique page title that includes the product name, the type and the brand, for example "Composite Hockey Stick 36.5 | Brand"
- A search description that says who it's for and why it's different, not a copy of the manufacturer's text
- Clear images with descriptive alt text
- Sizes, materials and care details in plain text, not only in an image
- Customer reviews on the page, so shoppers and search engines see real feedback

## Collection and category pages
Collections such as "junior cricket bats" or "club training wear" often rank better than individual products, because they match how people search. Give each one a short, useful introduction and its own title and description.

## Structured data
Structured data tells search engines exactly what's on the page. For a store, the essentials are:

1. Product, with price, currency and availability
2. Aggregate rating, from your customer reviews
3. Shipping details and returns, where you offer them
4. Breadcrumbs, so results show where the page sits in your store
5. FAQ, on pages that answer common questions

Done well, this is what turns a plain blue link into a result with stars, price and stock.

## Technical basics
- An XML sitemap that updates when products are added or removed
- Canonical URLs, so filtered and sorted versions of a collection don't compete with each other
- Fast pages on mobile, measured with Google's Core Web Vitals
- Pages for ended campaigns either redirected or removed from search

## Search on social and in AI assistants
Shoppers increasingly ask an AI assistant rather than a search engine. Help them describe you accurately: clear product content, structured data, and a short llms.txt file that explains what your store sells and who it's for.

When product links are shared on social media or in messaging apps, Open Graph tags decide the image and title people see. Check them before every campaign.

## Track what matters
Connect Google Analytics 4 with a cookie consent banner, and watch organic search revenue, not only traffic. A page that ranks well but doesn't sell needs better content or better products, not more SEO.

See what's built into every StacCraft store on our [commerce features page](#commerce.marketing).

article.author: StacCraft team
article.excerpt: Reviews lift conversion and search visibility, but the ACCC is clear about what businesses can't do with them. How to collect, moderate and display reviews properly.

sections.standfirst: Customer reviews are one of the strongest signals a shopper sees before buying. In Australia, they're also covered by the Australian Consumer Law, and the ACCC has taken action against businesses that mishandled them.
takeaways: Never write, buy or invent reviews
Don't hide or delay negative reviews because they're negative
Disclose any incentive offered for a review
Set a written moderation policy, and apply it to positive and negative reviews alike
sections.body:
## Why reviews matter
Reviews do three jobs at once. They help shoppers choose the right size and product, they give search engines fresh content and star ratings to show in results, and they tell you what to fix. For apparel and teamwear, fit and sizing comments are often the most valuable feedback a brand receives.

## What the law expects
The Australian Consumer Law prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct, and the ACCC treats the misuse of reviews as exactly that. In practice, a business should not:

- Write fake reviews, or ask staff, friends or agencies to write them
- Remove, hide or delay genuine negative reviews because they're negative
- Show only selected reviews in a way that gives a misleading overall impression
- Offer incentives for positive reviews only, or fail to disclose that a review was incentivised

> This article is general information, not legal advice. Check the ACCC's current guidance for businesses on online reviews before setting your policy.

## A moderation policy that's fair
Moderation is allowed and sensible, as long as the rules don't depend on whether a review is positive. A simple policy:

1. Publish reviews that relate to the product and the customer's experience
2. Remove reviews containing abuse, personal information, spam or content that isn't about the product
3. Apply the same rules to five-star and one-star reviews
4. Keep a record of what was removed and why

## Collecting more genuine reviews
- Ask after delivery, when the customer has worn or used the product
- Make it quick: rating first, comments optional
- Let customers add photos, which are especially helpful for fit
- Mark reviews from confirmed buyers as verified purchases
- Reply publicly to critical reviews, explaining what you'll do about the problem

## How StacCraft handles reviews
Reviews are built into every StacCraft store: star ratings, photos, verified-purchase badges, one review per customer per product, helpful votes, approval before publishing and public replies from your team. Ratings are added to product structured data so search engines can show them. [See reviews on the commerce page](#commerce.reviews).

pages.navLabel: Size runs and colourways: managing apparel variants at scale
pages.description: How apparel brands can structure products, sizes, colourways and fits so the catalogue, stock and purchasing all scale cleanly.

article.author: StacCraft team
article.excerpt: Variant limits, messy size data and per-size buying are the quiet problems of apparel ecommerce. How to structure a catalogue that scales.

sections.standfirst: A single playing shirt in eleven sizes, four colours and three fits is 132 variants. Multiply that by a range, and catalogue structure becomes a business decision, not an admin task.
takeaways: Design your size and colour structure before you load products
Use the same size codes everywhere: catalogue, stock and purchase orders
Buy in the size breakdown you sell, not in averages
Don't let platform variant limits shape your range
sections.body:
## Start with structure
Before loading a single product, agree on three things across sales, buying and the warehouse:

1. **Size scales.** Youth and adult sizes, numeric and letter sizes, and how they sort
2. **Colourways.** Named consistently, with the same codes your suppliers use
3. **Fits.** Men's, women's and youth as an option on one product, or separate products

Getting this right once saves thousands of fixes later, because every report, purchase order and stock count depends on it.

## Watch for variant limits
Many hosted ecommerce platforms cap how many variants or options a product can have. When a range outgrows the cap, teams split one product into several, which breaks reviews, search rankings and reporting. Check the limits of any platform before you commit to it.

## Show sizes the way shoppers choose them
- Show only the sizes that exist for the selected colour and fit
- Put size guides next to the size picker, not in a separate page
- Let returning customers see the size they bought last time

## Buy in the same breakdown you sell
The most expensive mistake in apparel buying is ordering by averages. If your customers bought 30 mediums and 9 extra-larges, your purchase order should say 30 and 9, not "77 units, standard curve". Purchase orders built from sales keep the size breakdown intact all the way to the supplier's production workbench.

## Plan drops and pre-orders
Launches, drops and pre-orders work best when the product, its availability dates and its purchase orders are planned together. Set the window, sell, close, and buy exactly what sold.

This policy covers personal information we collect through this website, and when you contact us by email or phone.

It doesn't cover the stores, club portals and dealer portals that businesses run on the StacCraft platform. Each of those businesses has its own privacy policy, which explains how it handles its customers' information. See "Information we handle for businesses on our platform" below.

You can browse this website without telling us who you are (APP 2). To reply to an enquiry or send you Insights, we need at least your name and an email address.

## How we use it
We use your personal information to:

- Reply to your enquiry and talk to you about our services
- Send you Insights articles and news, if you've asked us to
- Understand how the site is used, so we can improve it
- Keep the site secure and prevent misuse

We only use your information for the purpose we collected it for, or a related purpose you'd reasonably expect. We won't use it for anything else without your consent, unless the law requires or allows it (APP 6).

## Marketing emails
We only send marketing emails if you've agreed to receive them (APP 7). Every marketing email tells you who it's from and includes an unsubscribe link. We action unsubscribe requests within 5 business days, as required by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth).

You can also ask us to stop at any time by emailing [info@staccraft.com.au](mailto:info@staccraft.com.au). We never sell or give your details to other businesses for their own marketing.

## Cookies and analytics
This site uses Google Analytics only if you allow it in the cookie banner. You can change your choice at any time using "Cookie settings" in the footer. We don't use advertising cookies on this site.

## Who we share it with
We don't sell personal information. We share it only with service providers that help us run our business, such as:

- Microsoft 365, our email provider, which receives the messages you send us, including through our contact form
- Microsoft Azure, which hosts this website and keeps standard server logs, such as IP addresses
- Google Analytics, to understand how the site is used, only if you've allowed it

These providers may only use your information to provide their services to us. We may also share information with our professional advisers, or where the law requires or authorises it.

## Overseas disclosure
Google may process information outside Australia, including in the United States. Before we share personal information with an overseas provider, we take reasonable steps to make sure it's handled in line with the Australian Privacy Principles (APP 8).

## Automated decisions
We don't use personal information collected through this website to make decisions by computer program that could significantly affect your rights or interests. Enquiries are read and answered by our team. If this changes, we'll update this policy before it does, as the Privacy Act will require from December 2026.

## How we protect and keep it
We take reasonable steps to protect personal information from misuse, interference, loss, and unauthorised access, change or disclosure (APP 11). This website uses HTTPS, and access to enquiries is limited to the people in our team who need it.

We keep personal information only for as long as we need it for the purposes above, or as the law requires. After that, we delete it or de-identify it.

## Data breaches
If we suspect a data breach, we act quickly to contain it and assess it within 30 days. If it's likely to cause serious harm, we'll tell the people affected and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC), as required by the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme.

## Information we handle for businesses on our platform
Businesses that use the StacCraft platform collect information from their own customers, clubs, dealers and suppliers. We store and process that information on their behalf, only to provide the platform to them, and each business keeps its data in its own separate database.

If you're a customer of a store that runs on StacCraft, its privacy policy applies, and you should contact that business first about your information. We'll help the business respond to your request, and we'll tell it promptly if a data breach affects its store.

## Accessing and correcting your information
You can ask for a copy of the personal information we hold about you, or ask us to correct it if it's wrong, out of date or incomplete (APPs 12 and 13). Email [info@staccraft.com.au](mailto:info@staccraft.com.au). We won't charge you for making a request, and we'll respond within 30 days.

We may need to confirm your identity first. If we can't give you access or make a correction, we'll tell you why in writing, and how you can complain.

## Complaints
If you have a concern about how we've handled your personal information, please email us first at [info@staccraft.com.au](mailto:info@staccraft.com.au). We'll acknowledge it promptly and respond within 30 days.

If you're not satisfied with our response, you can complain to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner at [oaic.gov.au](https://www.oaic.gov.au) or on 1300 363 992.
